html:
The mass killing and expulsion of the Circassians, a people of the northwest Caucasus, by the Russian Empire at the end of its conquest of their land in 1864. Most Circassians were killed, died on the way, or were driven across the Black Sea to the Ottoman Empire.

The Circassians lived on the coast and in the valleys of the northwest Caucasus. They resisted Russian expansion for decades in the Russo-Circassian War. Under Tsar Alexander II the war was declared over in May 1864.

Hundreds of thousands were crowded onto boats to Ottoman ports; many died of hunger, cold and disease on the shore and at sea. Numbers are uncertain, but most estimates run to several hundred thousand dead and over a million expelled. Those who reached Ottoman lands were settled across Anatolia, the Balkans and the Levant (Circassian exodus to Ottoman lands).

Large Circassian communities live today in Turkey, Jordan and Syria. Georgia's parliament recognised the events as genocide in 2011. Russia does not.
